scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Dancers, known as danzaq, perform for up to ten hours in a competition called Atipanakuy, often testing their physical limits with acrobatic feats while wielding two independent metal plates.
This is Danza de las Tijeras. Pre-Hispanic origins.
on_screen: Title card: Danza de las Tijeras · Peru · Pre-Hispanic origins

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originates from the Chanka region.
Dancers descend from pre-Hispanic 'tusuq laykas'—priests and healers who were persecuted during the colonial period.
They were forced to adapt their rituals to Catholic festivals, leading to a syncretic tradition that persists today.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed during the dry season and coincides with important agricultural calendar phases.
It serves as a ritual offering to the 'Huamani' (mountain spirits) and other Andean deities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a competitive format called Atipanakuy.
Dancers perform in turns, executing steps that increase in risk and complexity.
The sequence includes 'Marcha' (walking on toes), 'Ensayo' (the start of the duel), and 'Tuku Mayor' (acrobatic feats).
Watch for Atipanakuy.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Competitive duel format; dancers perform in turns.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is provided by a duo of a harpist and a violinist.
The central instrument is the pair of metal scissors, consisting of two independent plates that are struck together to create a rhythmic sound.
Listen for the Harp, Violin, Metal scissors (two plates).
The sound is defined by the melodic interplay of a harp and violin, punctuated by the sharp, rhythmic metallic clashing of the scissors.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear costumes decorated with gold stripes, sequins, and small mirrors.
They are traditionally prohibited from entering the interior of churches while wearing these costumes due to the belief that their skills result from a pact with the devil.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Peruvian writer José María Arguedas (1911-1969) is credited with immortalizing the danzaq in his literary works, most notably in the 1962 short story 'La agonía de Rasu Ñiti'.
In Apurímac, the dance is called 'Saqras'; in Ayacucho, the performer is a 'danzaq'; and in Huancavelica, the dancer is known as a 'Gala'.
The tradition is passed down orally from teacher to student, with training often beginning in early childhood.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is considered a magical-religious ritual. Dancers are traditionally forbidden from entering churches in their performance costumes due to the belief that their abilities stem from a pact with the devil.
